title: Hari Singh Nalwa
hook: his great general held the north-west frontier and died at Jamrud
tomorrow: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht

segments.voice: Yesterday, a modern army: European drill, Sikh command, and a king willing to learn; your line was learn from all. Today, one of the generals who led it.

Rocky hills. A narrow pass climbing west into the mountains: the Khyber. At its mouth stands a fort called Jamrud, and inside it a small garrison is waiting for a fight. Somewhere in the hills an army is coming down. The man responsible for this edge of the kingdom is a general whose name, the stories say, had become a word for nerve. When he falls, the fort still has to hold.
screen: `THE MOUTH OF THE KHYBER.` → `A SMALL GARRISON AT JAMRUD.` → `A NAME THAT MEANT NERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition explains Nalwa with a story: on a hunt, a tiger sprang at the young Hari Singh, and he fought it and killed it. Whether every detail is true or not, the name stuck to him like armor. Next, the job. Ranjit Singh's kingdom reached toward the mountains of the north-west, toward Peshawar and the Khyber. That edge was hard to hold: rough country, local powers with their own claims, and a kingdom in Kabul that claimed the same ground. Hari Singh Nalwa was sent to hold it. He governed, built forts and kept the passes. Then Jamrud. Tradition tells it like this. An Afghan army came down to the fort. Hari Singh rode out to relieve it and was mortally wounded in the fighting. As he lay dying, he asked his men to keep his death a secret, so that defenders and enemy alike would think he was still in command until help could arrive. They did, and tradition says the fort held. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the deen, a word some read as the helpless and some as the faith, and who would be cut to pieces before leaving the field. Some Sikhs hear that line in stories like this one. The story honors not glory or the size of the battle, but a man who stood at the edge so others could live behind it, and who even in dying thought about who would hold the line.
screen: `NALWA: A NAME FROM A TIGER STORY.` · `SENT TO HOLD THE NORTH-WEST.` · `KEEP MY DEATH A SECRET.` · `THE HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE FRONTIER HELD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who count on you right now, someone at home, a friend, a team, a class, and then your worst kind of day, tired and short on patience. Name plainly the one thing you would still do for them on that day, and feel your feet on the floor while you hold it; if you pray, Waheguru on each breath out.
Nalwa, the name a tiger fight gave Hari Singh, Ranjit Singh's general on the north-west frontier, who died at Jamrud and, tradition says, kept the fort holding even then. Today's word.
Your line: the frontier held. A name that meant nerve. That's day nine hundred fourteen.

chat.says: What is Hari Singh Nalwa remembered for at Jamrud?
options: Mortally wounded, tradition says, he had his death kept secret so the fort would hold.
Capturing Kabul in a single day, which ended all the fighting on the frontier.
Surrendering the fort to save his men, then riding home to Lahore in peace.
chat.meaning: Tradition says that as he lay dying he asked his men to keep his death secret until help came, and the fort held.
